subject: physics
title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
key_idea: Unstable nuclei emit α particles, β particles or γ rays. The three differ in charge, mass, ionising power and penetration. A decay equation balances nucleon number and charge on both sides.

blocks.text: An unstable nucleus becomes more stable by emitting radiation. This section covers what each type is and how far it travels.

items.meaning: Radiation that removes electrons from atoms it passes, leaving charged ions.
How far the radiation travels into a material before it is absorbed.
The antiparticle of the electron, with the same mass and a charge of +e.

items: **α radiation** is a helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons, charge +2e, mass 4 u.
**β⁻ radiation** is a fast electron, charge −e. A β⁺ particle is a positron, charge +e.
β particles have a tiny mass, about 1/1800 of a nucleon.
**γ radiation** is a high-energy photon from the nucleus. It has no charge and no mass.

values: Very long, intensity falls with distance

items: α particles are heavy and highly charged, so they ionise strongly and lose their energy in a few centimetres of air.
β particles are lighter and ionise less, so they travel further.
γ rays have no charge, so they ionise least and are the most penetrating.
A radiation that ionises strongly is absorbed quickly: strong ionisation and long range do not go together.
α is a helium nucleus, β is an electron or positron, γ is a photon.
Ionising power falls from α to β to γ, while penetration rises.
γ is never fully stopped. Thick lead only reduces its intensity.

blocks.text: Radiation is all around us, so every measurement must be corrected. This section covers the sources of background and how to identify a source by absorption.

items.meaning: The ionising radiation always present from natural and artificial sources.
The measured count rate with the background count rate subtracted.

items: Natural sources: radon gas from rocks, cosmic rays, rocks and soil, food and drink, and the human body.
Artificial sources: medical procedures, fallout from weapons testing and the nuclear industry.
To remove it, measure the count rate with no source present, then subtract it from every reading.

items.text: Record the count rate on a Geiger–Müller tube and counter with the source removed.
Place the source a set distance from the tube, then place different absorbers between them.
Take the count rate with each absorber and subtract the background.
Paper stops α. A few mm of aluminium stops β. Only thick lead greatly reduces γ.

items: If paper cuts the count rate to background, the source is an α emitter.
If paper has little effect but aluminium does, the source emits β.
If only lead reduces it, the source emits γ. A mixed source gives a drop at each stage.
The same idea is used in thickness gauges: β radiation through paper or foil, γ radiation through steel. A change in count rate means a change in thickness.
Safe handling: use tongs, keep the source pointed away, store it in a lead-lined box and keep exposure short.
Always subtract the background count rate to get the corrected count rate.
The material that stops a radiation identifies it.
Thickness gauges use the way a material absorbs radiation.

blocks.text: A decay equation shows the parent nucleus, the daughter nucleus and the particle emitted. This section covers how to write and balance one.

items: Nucleon number A is written at the top left of the symbol, proton number Z at the bottom left.
The total A is the same before and after the decay.
The total charge (the sum of Z) is the same before and after the decay.
In β⁻ decay a neutron changes to a proton: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.
In β⁺ decay a proton changes to a neutron: p → n + e⁺ + νₑ.
γ emission changes neither A nor Z. The nucleus only loses energy.

diagram.alt: Pick a type of decay to see how the nucleon number and proton number of the nucleus change.

items: Balance A and Z on both sides of every decay equation.
α lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ raises Z by 1. β⁺ lowers Z by 1.
γ emission changes neither A nor Z.

checks.q: A source's count rate falls to the background level when a sheet of paper is placed in front of it. State the type of radiation emitted and explain your answer.
checks.a: α radiation, because α particles are strongly ionising and are absorbed by paper, whereas β and γ would pass through it.

checks.q: Complete the equation for the decay of radium-226 by α emission: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ?Rn + ⁴₂α.
checks.a: ²²²₈₆Rn. The nucleon number falls from 226 to 222 and the proton number from 88 to 86.

checks.q: State the change in the nucleus, and the particles emitted, in β⁻ decay.
checks.a: A neutron changes into a proton, and an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted. The proton number rises by 1 and the nucleon number is unchanged.

blocks.text: The inverse-square law for γ radiation
γ rays from a small source spread out in all directions, so their intensity falls quickly with distance.

blocks.label: Inverse-square law
where: I = intensity, or corrected count rate
k = a constant for the source
x = distance from the source in m

items: Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.
To verify the law, measure the corrected count rate at several distances and plot it against 1/x². A straight line through the origin confirms it.
The distance is measured to the tube, so keep the source small and well away from the tube.
For safe handling, keep a long distance from a source and spend as little time near it as possible.
On a graph of neutron number N against proton number Z, stable nuclei lie along a narrow band.
Light stable nuclei have N ≈ Z. Heavier ones have more neutrons than protons.
A nucleus above the band has too many neutrons and decays by **β⁻** emission.
A nucleus below the band has too few neutrons and decays by **β⁺** emission or electron capture.
Large nuclei beyond the band decay by α emission, which lowers both N and Z.
After α or β decay the daughter nucleus is often in an excited state and then emits a γ photon.
A nuclear energy level diagram shows the excited state above the ground state. The γ photon carries the energy difference between the two levels.
Technetium-99m is a pure γ source with a half-life of about 6 hours. It is used as a tracer in medical diagnosis.
Medical uses of radiation are a balance between the benefit of a diagnosis or treatment and the risk of exposure.
Outside the body, β and γ are the greater hazard because they penetrate skin. Inside the body, α is the most hazardous because it deposits all its energy in a small volume of tissue.

blocks.text: Energies of α and β particles

items: α particles from one type of nucleus have discrete energies. Each decay releases the same energy, shared between the α particle and the daughter nucleus.
β particles have a continuous range of energies, from zero up to a maximum.
This is because the energy is shared between the β particle and an (anti)neutrino, in a different split each time.
The continuous β spectrum was the evidence that a third particle, the neutrino, must be emitted.
